items.title: Anat Cohen interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 9, 2021
items.q: It’s a Dr. Lonnie Smith song, a very simple minor eight bars, the song is just powerful and simple like many songs.

ctx.x: Thanks for sharing that. I love that story. And speaking of important people the tune with Paquito D’Rivera was called “And the World Weeps.” And I’ve been in a situation a couple of times in my life where I was playing next to someone I really admired or was a mentor or teacher. And I was wondering if you were thinking, because he soloed first, and beautifully, did you allow yourself to have these kind of somewhat negative thoughts like what am I going to do now? You know I would have done what he did but he…

I just, you know I just have a different approach because what would I do now, for me, is a positive thought, not a negative thought. Because if he played something and he left me to a point, say a challenge, what do I have to add? How can I add to the music after everything that he already gave? So for me it’s not like oh my God he played so beautiful now I’m going to — I mean there’s no time and no room for negative thoughts at this point, it’s only about think about the music and you have to really be —…

definitely somebody I admire so much and it was such a thrill to have him, it was the D.C. Jazz Festival and actually he recorded that tune with me on my album Ciaroscuro, that “And the World Weeps.” It’s a Dr. Lonnie Smith song, a very simple minor eight bars, the song is just powerful and simple like many songs. And it’s just great because it can really show how for me how to be connected with your soul and how the clarinet can be so expressive and get such a wide range of emotions. And Pacquito is such an…
